title: SQL Injection
oneLiner: When user input gets pasted into SQL text, the user gets to write part of your query.
keyTakeaway: Never build SQL by gluing strings together with user input. Use parameterized queries -- ? or @name placeholders with the values passed separately -- so input is always treated as data, never as SQL. ORMs like EF Core do this for you, until you reach for raw SQL.
explanation:
A login check is often written as one query: find a user with this username and this password. Build it by pasting the form fields into a string, and the query's structure now depends on what the user typed. Type a quote and you've closed the string early; everything after it is read as SQL. `' OR '1'='1` turns "the password matches" into "the password matches OR one equals one", which is always true. `admin' --` comments out the password check entirely. And because many database drivers run several statements at once, `'; DROP TABLE users; --` can delete the table outright.

The fix is not escaping quotes by hand or blocking suspicious words -- attackers have decades of tricks for getting around both. The fix is a parameterized query. The SQL is sent with placeholders (`WHERE username = ? AND password = ?`) and the values are sent separately. The database parses the SQL first, so its structure is fixed before any input arrives; the input can only ever fill a value slot. Turn on "parameterized" in the demo and try every attack again.

In C#, that means `command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@name", name)` with ADO.NET, or just using EF Core's LINQ queries, which are parameterized automatically. Watch for the escape hatches: EF Core's `FromSqlRaw` with string concatenation is as vulnerable as any other string-built query (`FromSqlInterpolated` and `FromSql` parameterize for you). The same idea applies beyond SQL -- shell commands, LDAP filters, file paths -- anywhere input is mixed into something that gets interpreted.

Also note this demo's other mistake: passwords stored in plain text. See Hashing vs. Encryption for why that's a separate disaster.
